==Interiors and collections==
===Introduction===
Ham House is unusual in retaining much of its original 17th-century interior decoration, offering a rare experience of the style of the courts of Charles I and [[Stuart Restoration|Charles II]].{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=IX}} Ham House's rooms display collections of 17th-century paintings, [[Portrait painting|portraits]] and [[Portrait miniature|miniatures]], in addition to [[Cabinetry|cabinets]], [[Tapestry|tapestries]] and furniture amassed and retained by generations of the Murray and Tollemache families. Geoffrey Beard, in his study, ''The National Trust Book of English Furniture'', noted the extraordinarily high quality of the Lauderdales' furnishing of the house, undertaken with "a lavishness which transcended even what was fitting to their exalted rank".{{sfn|Beard|1985|p=96}} [[Bridget Cherry]], in the ''London: South'' volume of the [[Pevsner Architectural Guides]] suggested that, while the exterior of Ham was "not as attractive as other houses of this period", the "high architectural and decorative interest" of its interior should be recognised.{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=474}} John Julius Norwich considered the interiors, a "time machine – enclosing one in the elegant, opulent world of [[Anthony van Dyck|van Dyck]] and [[Peter Lely|Lely]]".{{sfn|Norwich|1985|p=360}}

===Great Hall===
[[File:The Great Hall at Ham House-geograph-3664352.jpg|thumb|The Great Hall from the Round Gallery|alt=A photograph looking down on the interior of the Great Hall, showing the chequerboard floor tiles, several of the large wall portraits and pieces of furniture placed at the edges of the room.]]
This room forms part of the original 1610 construction and is off-set from the centre, in the [[Gothic architecture|English Gothic]] and [[Tudor architecture|Tudor]] tradition.{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=475}} During this time, the hall may have been used for both dining and entertainment.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=38}} The distinctive black and white [[marble]] [[Checkerboard|chequerboard]] flooring is also believed to date from the original construction.{{sfn|Greeves|2008|pp=153–155}} By the early 18th century the room had been expanded upwards by opening the ceiling to the room above, now known as the Round Gallery. The room contains a number of large and notable paintings.

* ''Charlotte Walpole, Countess of Dysart (1738–1789)'', by Sir [[Joshua Reynolds]], was exhibited at the [[Royal Academy of Arts|Royal Academy]] in 1775.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139646|title=Charlotte Walpole, Countess of Dysart (1738–1789) – Item NT1139646|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>
* John Constable, a family friend, was commissioned to make copies of two family portraits: ''Anna Maria Lewis, Countess of Dysart (1745–1804)'' as Miranda, painted in 1823 after Joshua Reynolds<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1140004|title=Anna Maria Lewis, Countess of Dysart (1745–1804) – Item NT1140004|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref> and ''Lady Louisa Tollemache, Countess of Dysart (1745–1840)'', painted in 1823–25 after [[John Hoppner]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1140003|title=Lady Louisa Tollemache, Countess of Dysart (1745–1840) – Item NT1140003|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>
* Hanging side by side are [[John Vanderbank]]'s portraits of ''Lionel Tollemache, 4th Earl of Dysart (1708–1770)'' painted in 1730<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139649|title=Lionel Tollemache, 4th Earl of Dysart (1708–1770) – Item NT1139649|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref> and of his wife ''Lady Grace Carteret, Countess of Dysart (1713–1755)'', signed and dated 1737.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139647|title=Lady Grace Carteret, Countess of Dysart (1713–1755) – Item NT1139647|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>

===Chapel===
[[File:Ham house chapel.jpg|thumb|The Chapel|alt=A photograph of the small family chapel, with wooden panelling and red wall hangings]]
Formerly the family's sitting room, this room was converted to a chapel during the major renovations of the 1670s.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=96}} It was decorated with crimson [[velvet]] and [[damask]] wall hangings, which were changed to black velvet upon the Duke's death in 1682.{{sfn|NT|2009|pp=12–13}} While designed for Protestant worship, the chapel was used in the late 19th century by the wife of the 8th Earl for Roman Catholic services.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=370}} The sumptuous and rare 17th-century [[textiles]] require that the light levels remain low, in order to minimise damage.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|pp=97–99}}

===Great Staircase===
[[File:Ham house stairs 4.jpg|thumb|Panelling and fruit basket newel posts on the Great Staircase|alt=A photograph of the dark wooden panelling of the staircase, engraved with military symbols, and the carved baskets of fruit which sit atop the newel post at the bottom of the baluster]]
The Great Staircase, described by the historian Christopher Rowell as "remarkable" and "apparently without a close parallel in the British Isles",{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=73}} was created for William Murray at the east end of the Great Hall in 1638–39 as part of a series of improvements to the house which reflected his rising status at Court.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=5}} An ornately carved archway marks the entrance from the Great Hall to the stairs, which were designed as a grand processional route giving access to the State Apartments on the first floor.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=4}} The [[cantilever]] staircase rises over three floors above a square stairwell. The balustrade is composed of boldly hand-carved pierced wooden panels depicting trophies of war.{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=476}} Each panel is different, with varying images on each face of arms and armour, including a set of [[Barding|horse armour]]. The wide range of arms includes [[field gun]]s with cannonballs and barrels of [[gunpowder]], swords, shields, [[quiver]]s of arrows and [[halberd]]s. Dolphins, elephant heads, dragons and other fantastical creatures also appear on the [[Dado (architecture)|dado]] panelling, together with military drums and trumpets. The martial theme of these panels is interspersed with drops of [[relief carving]]s of bay leaves, richly carved [[newel]] posts topped with baskets of fruit{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=476}} designed to carry candles or [[candelabra]], and miniature [[Festoon|swags]] decorating the outer [[Belt course|string]]. Originally gilded and [[Graining|grained]] to resemble [[walnut]],{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=75}} in the 19th century the balustrade and other woodwork were picked out in bronze, traces of which survive. According to Rowell, "There is no other architectural wood carving on this scale and of such sophistication surviving from the late 1630s."{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=73}}

A collection of 17th century copies of old master paintings in their original carved frames hangs on the staircase wall. Two were copied from originals in the collection of Charles I:{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=101}} ''[[Venus with Mercury and Cupid]]'' (The ''School of Love'') by [[Correggio]] at the base of the stairs (the original in the [[National Gallery]], London),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139671|title=Venus with Mercury and Cupid (The School of Love) – Item NT1139671|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref> while on the first floor landing there is a copy of ''[[Pardo Venus|The Venus Del Pardo (Venus and a Satyr)]]'' by [[Titian]] (the original in the [[Louvre]], Paris).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139666|title=The Venus Del Pardo (Venus and a Satyr) – Item NT1139666|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>

===Round Gallery===
Before the upward expansion of the Great Hall this room had served as the Great Dining Room, as created by William Murray in the 1630s.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=22}} The ornate white [[stucco|plasterwork]] ceiling was created by Joseph Kinsman,{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=476}} master craftsman and member of [[Worshipful Company of Plaisterers|the London Plasterers' Company]].{{sfn|Jackson-Stops|1979|p=23}} Engaged by the [[Office of Works|Royal Works]] at [[Goldsmith's Hall]], [[Palace of Whitehall|Whitehall]] and [[Somerset House]], he was employed by William Murray at Ham House during the 1637 renovation and creation of the State Apartments.{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=476}} The ceilings at Ham are the only surviving example of his work, showing the influence of Inigo Jones in their design of deep [[Beam (structure)|beams]] with [[Rosette (design)|rosettes]] at the intersections, enclosing geometric compartments.{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=476}} The white plaster high relief oval swags of luscious fruit, flowers and ribbons, including the odd worm, contrasted with the elaborate [[frieze]] which was originally coloured blue and gold.{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=476}}

Notable paintings include [[Peter Lely]]'s final portrait of Elizabeth, painted c. 1680, and the earlier double portrait, ''John Maitland, Duke of Lauderdale and Elizabeth Murray, Countess of Dysart and Duchess of Lauderdale'' painted by Lely c. 1675.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139789|title=John Maitland, Duke of Lauderdale (1616–1682) and Elizabeth Murray, Countess of Dysart and Duchess of Lauderdale (1626–1698) – Item NT1139789|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>

===North Drawing Room===
[[File:View of the North Drawing Room.JPG|thumb|The North Drawing Room|alt=A photograph of a richly-decorated room, with a white marble fireplace surrounded by elaborate wall carvings of twisted pillars and scrolling foliage. The ceiling is also decorated with plaster fruit and flowers. Tapestries line the walls, and a set of satin-covered chairs are placed at the edge of the room.]]
After dinner in the adjacent dining room, guests would have retired to the North Drawing Room for conversation.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=24}} This room was decorated at the same time as the Great Dining Room, and was later hung with tapestries.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=24}} Kinsman continued his elaborate plasterwork in the white ceiling in this room.{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=476}} Deep beams enclose rectangles bursting with individually crafted fruit and flowers. The hemispherical rosettes at the intersections are unusual, possibly unique.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=56}}

A notable piece of furniture in this room is the ivory cabinet: [[Wood veneer|veneered]] in rippled [[ivory]] panels on the exterior and the interior, this large oak and [[List of plants known as cedar|cedar]] cabinet opens to reveal 14 drawers. An inner door conceals small drawers, further secret drawers and a compartment. It was recorded as being moved to the prestigious Queen's Bedchamber shortly after its appearance in the 1677 inventory{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=34}} and is considered the most impressive piece of furniture designed or bought for the house (with the exception of the [[Baldachin#State bed|State Bed]], which no longer exists).{{sfn|Thornton|1980|p=241}} The cabinet may have been made in the Northern Netherlands based on furniture [[inlay|inlaid]] in ivory brought back in 1644 by [[John Maurice, Prince of Nassau-Siegen]], the former Governor of [[Dutch Brazil]] for his home in The Hague, now called the [[Mauritshuis]].{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=34}} 
   
Also notable in the room are a vibrant set of tapestries. James I established the [[Mortlake Tapestry Works]] in 1619 just three miles from Ham House, from which the Lauderdales had purchased a set of tapestries showing the seasons incorporating [[Tapestry#Production|gold thread]] for the Queen's Bedchamber.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=183}} While these are no longer at the house, the 4th Earl of Dysart acquired a set woven in Lambeth in 1699–1719 by the ex-Mortlake weaver Stephen de May, probably to the Mortlake design.{{sfn|NT|2009|p=20}} Altered to hang in the North Drawing Room, this set of ''The Seasons'' was originally commissioned by the [[John Petty, 1st Earl of Shelburne|1st Lord Shelburne]].{{sfn|NT|2009|p=20}} Tapestries were important in Europe for comfort in draughty manor houses and as status objects because of their expense.  Sets with designs showing the seasons or months were popular and had a number of variations depicting appropriate seasonal activities{{sfn|Standen|1971|p=5}} such as milking for April, ploughing and sowing for September, and wine-making for October.{{sfn|Ward|1953|p=114}}

===Long Gallery===
[[File:The Long Gallery at Ham House.jpg|thumb|The Long Gallery from the windows at the front of the house|alt=A photograph of a long dark room with high plain ceilings and gold-framed portraits lining the walls]]
The [[Long Gallery]] was part of the original 1610 house, but was extensively redecorated in 1639 by William Murray. It has been used as an exercise space as well as a gallery to showcase portraits of family and important royal connections.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=26}} Notable paintings include:

* ''Sir John Maitland, 1st Baron Maitland of Thirlestane (1543–1595), aged 44'' attributed to [[Adrian Vanson]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139943|title=Sir John Maitland, 1st Baron Maitland of Thirlestane (1543–1595), aged 44 – Item NT1139943|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref> In late 2016 an X-ray revealed that underneath the main painting was another, unfinished portrait likely of [[Mary, Queen of Scots]], dated 1589—two years after her execution. According to the National Trust, this painting "shows that portraits of the queen were being copied and presumably displayed in Scotland around the time of her execution, a highly contentious and potentially dangerous thing to be seen doing".<ref>{{cite web |title=Revealing Ham House's Hidden Portrait of Mary, Queen of Scots |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/revealing-ham-houses-hidden-portrait-of-mary-queen-of-scots |publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>
* ''King Charles I (1600–1649)'' by Sir Anthony van Dyck and studio.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=145}} In recognition of their friendship this painting was given by Charles I to William Murray; a 1638–39 memorandum of pictures bought by the King from Van Dyck includes framed pictures, one of which is believed to be this portrait.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139944|title=King Charles I (1600–1649) – Item NT1139944|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>
*''Colonel The Hon. John Russell (1620–1681)'' by [[John Michael Wright]] is signed and dated 1659.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139947|title=Colonel The Hon. John Russell (1620–1681) – Item NT1139947|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>
* Of the 15 portraits by Peter Lely in Ham House,{{sfn|Waterhouse|1994|p=65}} 11 are hung in the Long Gallery. These include ''Elizabeth Murray with a Black Servant'', ''John Maitland, Duke of Lauderdale (1616–1682) in Garter robes'', and ''[[Thomas Clifford, 1st Baron Clifford of Chudleigh]] KG (1630–1673) in Garter robes''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139940|title=Elizabeth Murray with a Black Servant – Item NT1139940|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139952|title=John Maitland, Duke of Lauderdale (1616–1682) in Garter robes – Item NT1139952|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139953|title=Thomas Clifford, 1st Baron Clifford of Chudleigh KG (1630–1673) in Garter robes – Item NT1139953|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>

[[Picture frame]]s at Ham House date from the 17th century and its Long Gallery portraits are a showcase of elaborately carved, gilded frames in the [[auricular style]] (literally 'of the ear').{{sfn|Bracken|Gáldy|Turpin|2020|p=30}} Two frames date from the 1630s, ''Charles I'' and ''[[Henrietta Maria]]''. Later frames, for instance on the portraits of ''Elizabeth Murray with a Black Servant''{{efn|In 2020, the National Trust published a report on a survey completed to identify links between colonialism and the properties in its portfolio. The entry on Ham House noted that the Duke of Lauderdale was connected to organisations involved in [[colonialism]] and [[slavery]].<ref name="NT Slavery report">{{cite web |title=Interim Report on the Connections between Colonialism and Properties Now in the Care of the National Trust, Including Links with Historic Slavery |url=https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/documents/colionialism-and-historic-slavery-report.pdf |publisher=National Trust |access-date=18 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220318050716/https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/documents/colionialism-and-historic-slavery-report.pdf|archive-date= 18 March 2022}}</ref>}} and ''Lady Margaret Murray, Lady Maynard'' are in a similar auricular style with straight sight edges. These frames, referred to as Sunderland frames, are distinguished by their irregular sight edges. They take their name from the [[2nd Earl of Sunderland]], who displayed many pictures at his estate [[Althorp]] framed in this style.<ref>{{cite web |title=Framing in the Reign of Charles II and the Introduction of the Sunderland Frame |url=https://www.npg.org.uk/research/programmes/the-art-of-the-picture-frame/other-studies-charles-ii |publisher=National Portrait Gallery |access-date=20 August 2021}}</ref> There are examples of Sunderland frames on the portraits of ''John Maitland, Duke of Lauderdale (1616–1682) in Garter Robes''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139952|title=John Maitland, Duke of Lauderdale (1616–1682) in Garter Robes – Item NT1139952|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref> and ''Colonel The Hon. John Russell (1620–1681)''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1140913|title=Colonel The Hon. John Russell (1620–1681)[Frame] – Item NT1140913|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>

This room also displays some notable furniture:

* Floral marquetry cabinet: Ham House has a number of tables and cabinets decorated with floral marquetry including this, the earliest inventoried example in England, dating from 1675.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|pp=199–203}} The naturalistic representations of flowers and fruit are cut from contrasting woods such as ebony, walnut and stained fruitwood and laid onto the carcass. The woods and other materials were often dyed to create a greater range of colours and the green leaves on this piece are made from stained ivory or bone. This cabinet, as well as other tables and a mirror in the house, is attributed by the National Trust to [[William and Mary style|Gerrit Jensen]], who was the cabinet maker in ordinary to [[Catherine of Braganza]].{{sfn|Bowett|Lindey|2017|p=41}} 
* 
* [[Japanese lacquerware|Japanese lacquered]] cabinet: Japanese lacquered furniture was fashionable in the 17th century and this cabinet from 1650 remains in the Long Gallery where it has stood since then. Decorated with hills, trees and birds in raised gold and silver lacquer, the doors open on engraved brass hinges to reveal 10 drawers. The giltwood stand has four legs carved as elephant trunks topped with winged [[Putto|cherub]] busts.{{sfn|Thornton|1980|p=240}} 
* 
* [[Lacquerware#Chinese lacquerware|Chinese lacquered]] chest: China was another Asian source of lacquered furniture in the 17th century. Decorated with watery landscapes and branches, this chest is lacquered in gold and red on a dark crimson ground. It was a standard form of storage chest for linens and other textiles.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=183}} The English stand c. 1730 is [[japanned]], a technique developed by English and European craftsmen to approximate the hard, smooth and shiny surfaces of popular Asian lacquered goods.{{sfn|NT|2009|p=25}}

===Green Closet===
[[File:Green Closet fireplace at Ham House.jpg|thumb|The Green Closet|alt=A photograph of a richly-decorated room, covered in bright green silk damask over which several small paintings are hanging. A white marble fireplace and two lacquer cabinets are also visible.]]
Used for the display of miniature paintings and smaller-scale furniture, in contrast to the Long Gallery,{{sfn|Bracken|Gáldy|Turpin|2020|p=30}} this room is a very rare survival of a room in the style of Charles I's court.{{sfn|Greeves|2008|pp=153–155}} In the 1630s the Green Closet was specifically designed by William Murray to display miniatures and small paintings.{{sfn|Bracken|Gáldy|Turpin|2020|p=26}} The ceiling paintings are [[tempera]] on paper, and represent some of [[Francis Cleyn|Franz Cleyn's]] best surviving work.{{sfn|Jackson-Stops|1979|p=25}} Two preliminary drawings for the ''capricci'' of putti by Cleyn and an associate are held by the [[University of Southampton]].<ref>David Howarth, 'The Southampton Album: A Newly Discovered Collection of Drawings by Francis Cleyn the Elder and His Associates', ''Master Drawings'', 49:4 (Winter 2011), pp. 435-478.</ref>

Today it contains 87 items including ''Queen Elizabeth I (1533–1603)'' painted c. 1590 by [[Nicholas Hilliard]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1140182|title=Queen Elizabeth I (1533–1603) – Item NT1140182|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref> and ''A Man Consumed by Flames'' painted c. 1610 by [[Isaac Oliver]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139627|title=A Man consumed by Flames – Item NT1139627|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>

===Library===
[[File:The Library at Ham House-geograph-3664358.jpg|thumb|The Library|alt=A photograph of two walls containing bookshelves filled with antique volumes; in the foreground a set of globes and a map screen]]
The Library dates from the 1672–74 enlargement of the house. The architectural historian [[Mark Girouard]] considers it probably "the oldest country house library" still in existence.{{sfn|Girouard|1980|p=170}} Although some shelves were moved from what is now the Queen's Antechamber, most of the cedar fixed furniture, including the secretaire, was provided by Henry Harlow.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=68}} The Duke of Lauderdale added substantially to the contents: he was an avid reader and collector{{sfn|Bracken|Gáldy|Turpin|2020|p=36}} (so much so that his [[Lauderdale House|Highgate house]] was said to be in danger of collapse due to the weight of his substantial book collection),{{sfn|Cripps|1975|p=140}} and he owed huge sums to booksellers when he died. Mark Purcell, in his 2017 study ''The Country House Library'', notes that the probate inventory undertaken on the Duke's death estimated the value of his books at half of the total worth of the house's [[Personal property|chattels]].{{sfn|Purcell|2019|p=14}} Many volumes were sold at auctions between 1688 and 1692, in part due to the Duchess's money difficulties upon the Duke's death.{{sfn|NT|2009|p=29}}

Later members of the family rebuilt the collection, notably the 4th Earl who bought at the [[Harleian Library|Harleian auction]] and elsewhere.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=290}} He acquired 12 books printed by [[William Caxton]] and many other [[incunabula]];{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=15}} in 1904 a visitor, William Younger Fletcher, described the library as containing books of greater value, in proportion to its size, than any other in Europe.{{sfn|Roundell|1904|pp=133–140}} Most of the books were sold in 1938,{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=290}} and the bulk of the remainder after the Second World War. A notable exception, a [[Book of Common Prayer (1549)|Book of Common Prayer]] from [[Whitehall Palace]], is sometimes on display in the chapel.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|pp=32–36}}

After the war Norman Norris, a Brighton book dealer, assembled a collection of books from a range of post-war country house sales. He bequeathed the collection to the National Trust and many eventually came to Ham, primarily those pre-dating the mid-18th century.{{sfn|Attar|2016|p=170}} One, ''Jus Parliamentarium'', which has the Dysart coat of arms on its cover, is from the Dysart collection. The ceiling and friezes in the room display a lively [[Realism (arts)|naturalism]]. Two [[globe]]s with rare leather covers{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=135}} (acquired in 1745 and 1746) and two [[fire screen]]s (1743) are notable.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=292}}

===Queen's Apartments===
This suite of three rooms, now referred to as the Queen's Apartments, was created by the Duke and Duchess of Lauderdale when the house was enlarged in 1673.{{sfn|Greeves|2008|pp=153–155}} Intended for use by Catherine of Braganza,{{efn|[[Simon Jenkins]] suggests that the intended visit by Queen Catherine may not in fact have taken place,{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|pp=494–495}} although other sources indicate a visit in 1674.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=122}}}}{{sfn|Rothwell|Westman|2011|pp=7–8}} they reflect the latest innovations from France, where royalty received important visitors in the State Bedchamber.{{sfn|Bracken|Gáldy|Turpin|2020|p=29}} The rooms are decorated with increasing splendour, beginning with the relatively modest Antechamber, culminating in the small but richly gilded and decorated Queen's Closet.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=64}}

====Antechamber====
The first of the suite of rooms is the antechamber, where visitors would wait for an [[Audience (meeting)|audience]] with the Queen. The ceiling of this waiting room is the first of the three ceilings by the plasterer Henry Wells.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=61}} A circular [[garland]] of leaves is thickly studded with small flowers, surrounded by four [[spandrel]]s containing foliage and ribbons. The oak [[Parquetry|parquet]] floor, an innovation from France, continues through to the far side of the Queen's Bedchamber where it is then replaced with a more elaborate marquetry design where the State Bed would have stood. The blue velvet and damask wall hangings, installed during the period 1679–1683, are extremely rare survivals.{{sfn|Rothwell|Westman|2011|pp=3–4}}

====Queen's Bedchamber====
[[File:Queen's Bedchamber at Ham House.jpg|thumb|The Queen's Bedchamber, later converted to a sitting room|alt=A photograph of a richly-decorated room, with walls covered by tapestries and several pieces of sitting room furniture as well as an elaborately-carved ceiling]]
This room, built on the central axis of the house, was designed for the reception of guests and visiting dignitaries who would have waited to be summoned from the Antechamber. The State Bed stood prominently on a raised dais at the east end of the room facing the door.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=14}} A balustrade separated the bed from the main area of the room where visitors may have gathered for their audience with the Queen. The bed was on an elaborate marquetry floor inlaid with the [[Monogram|cipher]] and ducal [[coronet]] of the Duke and Duchess of Lauderdale, their initials J, E and L entwined in cedar and walnut, a feature that repeats in the Queens's Closet.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=143}} The floor remains in excellent condition. This ceiling has the richest plaster decoration in the house, a large deep oval of bay leaves dotted with roses. These cluster more densely at the east end, above the area of the Queen's State Bed. The spandrels are also more decorative, [[Acanthus (ornament)|acanthus]] leaves swirl to fill the panels, each corner hiding a [[grotesque]] figure among the foliage or bursting from the flowers.{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=477}}

The bed had been removed by 1728{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=181}} and the rooms were closed and rarely used, contributing to their excellent state of preservation. The change of use to a drawing room took place in the mid‑18th century with the lowering of the dais in line with the rest of the floor, and the purchase of new furniture and a set of William Bradshaw's popular early 18th century [[pastoral]] tapestries.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=181}} Woven in 1734–40 for [[Henry O'Brien, 8th Earl of Thomond]], and purchased in 1742 for £184 on behalf of the 4th Earl of Dysart, the tapestries needed only slight alterations to fit three of the walls of his newly decorated drawing room. Bradshaw's signature can be seen on The ''Dance'' tapestry. Woven in [[Soho]], London, the four wool and silk tapestries have narrow borders in the style of picture frames and are thought to incorporate several different images from works by the French painters [[Antoine Watteau]], [[Nicolas Lancret]] and [[Jean-Baptiste Pater]].{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=18}}

====Queen's Closet====
The smallest, most intimate of the suite of rooms, the third and final room was designed for private use and could be closed off, away from the business of the State Bedchamber.{{efn|[[Jeremy Musson]], in his study ''How the Read a Country House'', references the closets at Ham as among the "finest" late-17th century examples, and notes the derivation of the modern term [[Cabinet (government)|cabinet government]] from Charles II's use of such closets, or cabinets, to discuss confidential matters.{{sfn|Musson|2005|p=160}}}} Rarely used and preserved largely intact, the decoration, textiles and furniture give a unique record of late 17th century interior decoration.{{sfn|Rothwell|Westman|2011|p=3}} The marquetry floor incorporating the ducal coronet and cipher continues from the Bedchamber into the Closet. The ceiling painting of [[Ganymede Abducted by the Eagle|Ganymede and the Eagle]] is in the style of the Italian artist [[Antonio Verrio]] (1636–1707).{{sfn|Brett|2009|p=6}} Framed by a plaster garland,{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=477}} following the designs of the previous rooms, the richness of the effect is emphasised by gilding of the roses. Three ceiling paintings, again in the style of Verrio,{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=152}} of cupids sprinkling flowers, are partly hidden from view above the alcove. The elaborate chimney piece, hearth and windowsill, again including the Lauderdale cipher and ducal coronet, are made from [[scagliola]], possibly the earliest documented example of scagliola in this country.{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=477}}

===Private Closet===
[[File:Private Closet Ham House.jpg|thumb|The Duchess's Private Closet|alt=A photograph of a room decorated in green wallpaper, with several pieces of wooden furniture as well as an arrangement of miniature black and white portraits]]
This was the Duchess's most private and intimate room where she would read, write and entertain her closest family and friends.{{sfn|Greeves|2008|pp=153-–155}} The elaborate oil on plaster ceilings in both of the Duchess's closets are by Antonio Verrio. They are among his earliest commissions in England, and his earliest surviving work following his arrival from France in 1672.{{sfn|Brett|2009|p=6}} As his reputation grew he was commissioned by royal and aristocratic clients for larger projects including for Charles II at Windsor Castle,{{sfn|Brett|2009|p=7}} interiors for the [[John Cecil, 5th Earl of Exeter|Earl of Exeter]] at [[Burghley House]]{{sfn|Brett|2009|p=10}} and for [[William III of England|William III]] at Hampton Court.{{sfn|Brett|2009|pp=11–12}} The ceiling painting of ''The Penitent Magdalene Surrounded by Putti Holding Emblems of Time, Death and Eternity'' was completed around 1675.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=127}} The central figure floats above the room, circled by three [[putto|putti]] carrying symbols of time (an hourglass), death (a skull), and eternity (a snake eating its own tail). Verrio linked the ceiling design to the room by enclosing it in a narrow painted grey marble surround, matching the marble fireplace.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=82}} The room also contains a portrait of ''Catherine Bruce, Mrs William Murray (d. 1649)'', by [[John Hoskins (painter)|John Hoskins the Elder]], a [[watercolour]] on [[vellum]] in an ebony travelling case, signed and dated 1638.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139682|title=Catherine Bruce, Mrs William Murray (d. 1649) – Item NT1139682|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>

===White Closet===
Adjoining the Private Closet and richly decorated, this room was used by the Duchess for relaxing and entertaining, its double glazed door leading out to the Cherry Garden.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=78}} The [[Moulding (decorative)|coved]] ceiling of this glamorous room, originally decorated with white silk hangings and marble effect walls,{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=77}} emphasises the advanced taste of the Duke and Duchess of Lauderdale in a room intended for their most important visitors.{{sfn|Bracken|Gáldy|Turpin|2020|p=36}} Painted by Verrio{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=476}} in oil on plaster in 1673/74, it is described by the art historians Peter Thornton and Maurice Tomlin as "decorated with one of the earliest examples of [[Baroque painting|Baroque]] [[Illusionism (art)|illusionism]] to have been executed in a domestic interior in this country".{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=81}} Putti climb up over a [[trompe l'oeil]] balustrade to reach the figures of ''Divine Wisdom Presiding Over The Liberal Arts'', represented by seven mainly female figures bearing the symbols of Verrio's version of the [[Liberal arts education#History|liberal arts]].{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=82}} The figure of Wisdom floats on clouds pointing to the [[Eye of Providence|all-seeing eye]] in the open sky above. Verrio linked the ceiling design to the room by enclosing it in a narrow painted red marble surround, matching the red marble fireplace,{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=78}} as in the Private Closet. The heavily gilded coving includes [[Medallion (architecture)|medallions]] of the four [[Cardinal virtues]]. Notable collection items include:

*''Ham House from the South'' (1675–79) by [[Hendrick Danckerts]] depicts a finely dressed couple (possibly the Duke and Duchess of Lauderdale) in front of the south front and formal gardens,{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=158}} and was set into the chimneypiece in the White Closet shortly after the building was completed.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139878|title=Ham House from the South (1675–79) – Item NT1139878|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>
*[[Secretary desk|Escritoire]] of [[Kingwood (wood)|kingwood]] oysterwork: this elegant oak scriptor (c. 1672–75) is veneered with South American [[Kingwood (wood)|kingwood]] using the [[oystering]] technique and features silver mounts. Made for the Duchess of Lauderdale, it is listed in the 1679 inventory of Ham House and is believed to have been made in London by a French or Dutch craftsman.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=65}} Kingwood was one of the most expensive woods used in furniture making in the 17th century.{{sfn|Beard|1985|p=46}}<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bonhams.com/auctions/21710/lot/3/?category=list|title=William and Mary kingwood oyster cabinet on stand|publisher=Bonhams|access-date=21 November 2021}}</ref>

===Marble Dining Room===
[[File:Marble Dining Room in Ham House.jpg|thumb|The Marble Dining Room|alt=A photograph of a large room with leather wall-hangings, wooden marquetry floors and a single table set for two persons]]
Since 1675 the walls of the Marble Dining Room have been decorated with [[Leather wallpaper|leather panels]].{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|pp=43–44}} Today visitors can see two distinct designs. The earlier design of 1675 complemented the original black and white marble floor, for which the room is named, with brightly coloured [[Flemish Baroque painting|Flemish]] leather panels of fruits and flowers such as tulips and roses mixed with birds and butterflies on a white background. These had been embossed and some elements gilded, giving the room a sumptuous look.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=43}}

In 1756, the 4th Earl removed the marble floor and replaced it with a fine marquetry floor of tropical [[hardwoods]].{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=290}} He also commissioned John Hutton of London to make a new set of leather wall hangings with an embossed [[Diapering|diaper]] rosette surrounded by four leaves.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=290}} The parts of the design which are now brown would originally have appeared to be gold, made by varnishing [[Metal leaf|silver leaf]] in yellow.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=44}} The fashion for leather wall decoration spread from Spain and the Spanish Netherlands in the 17th century and was considered ideal for dining rooms as leather did not become impregnated with the odours of food like the fabric of a tapestry.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=44}} The Ham House inventory of 1655 indicates the "two parlers facing the river were hung with gilt leather."{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=249}}

===Withdrawing Room===
[[File:Ham House Withdrawing Room.jpg|thumb|alt=A richly-furnished antechamber to the adjacent dining room, it contains paintings, porcelain jars, silk damask wall hangings and an elaborate cabinet on a stand.|The Withdrawing Room]]
After dining in the adjacent Marble Dining Room, guests would retire to this space for entertainment and conversation.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=67}} It also served as an antechamber to the adjacent bedchamber.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=67}} Notable in this room is the ebony and [[tortoiseshell]] cabinet:  this cabinet (c. 1650–1675) on a possibly 19th century stand features red tortoiseshell decoration on a somewhat austere ebonised pine exterior that does not prepare the viewer for the ornate interior. Two doors open to reveal multiple shallow drawers on either side of an architectural exterior, which then opens to a [[Theatrical scenery|theatrical set]] framed by golden pillars and mirrors.{{sfn|Thornton|1980|p=242}} Known as the Antwerp cabinet,{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=13}} it is embellished with ivory, [[Ruin marble|pietra paesina]] (a type of naturally patterned limestone) and gilt bronze and brass.{{sfn|NT|2009|p=40}}

===Duchess's Bedchamber===
Originally the Duke's bedchamber,{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=48}} it is believed it became the Duchess's bedchamber following the installation of the bathroom{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=48}} which is accessed via the door to the left of the bed alcove. The ceiling above the bed in the alcove is painted in the style of Antonio Verrio and shows the partially clothed ''Flora Attended by Cupids'' floating above the tester of the [[four poster bed]].{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=61}} The monogram initials J, E and L (John, Elizabeth, Lauderdale) are entwined in each corner. Notable paintings include:

* ''Elizabeth Murray (1626–1698)'' painted by Peter Lely in 1648, the year of her marriage to Lionel Tollemache.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139764|title=Elizabeth Murray (1626–1698) – Item NT1139764|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>
*   
* A set of four [[overdoor]] [[Marine painting|maritime paintings]] by [[Willem van de Velde the Younger]], signed and dated 1673, including ''Calm: An English Frigate at Anchor Firing a Salute'', which remain from the decoration scheme planned for the room's use as the Duke's bedchamber.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=53}}

===Back Parlour===
This was the room in which senior male staff would have eaten their meals and spent any free time.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=15}} Hanging in this room is: ''Elizabeth Murray, Countess of Dysart (1626–1698), with her First Husband, Sir Lionel Tollemache (1624–1669), and her Sister, Margaret Murray, Lady Maynard (c. 1638–1682)'' painted c. 1648 by [[Joan Carlile]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1139727|title=Elizabeth Murray, Countess of Dysart (1626–1698), with her First Husband, Sir Lionel Tollemache (1624–1669), and her Sister, Margaret Murray, Lady Maynard (c. 1638–1682) – Item NT1139727|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref> a friend and neighbour to the Murrays.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=6}}

==Garden and grounds==
[[File:Petersham Road Lodge - geograph.org.uk - 1176138.jpg|thumb|Petersham Road Lodge, the principal gatehouse on the approach to Ham House from the A307|alt=A photograph of a three-story brick building with a prominent archway in the centre surmounted by an elaborate carved crest. The sides of the building are topped by a set of triple chimney-stacks.]]
The gardens and pleasure grounds at Ham cover approximately {{convert|12|hectare}}. They follow an axial plan, with avenues originally leading east, west and south from the house. The fourth, northern, side of the estate fronts the River Thames.<ref name="auto">{{NHLE|num=1000282|desc=Ham House Park and Garden|grade=II*|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref> The listed avenues leading to the house from the [[A307 road|A307]] are formed by more than 250 trees stretching east from the house to the 19th-century [[Jacobethan]] gate house at Petersham, and south across the open expanse of [[Ham Common, London|Ham Common]] where it is flanked by a pair of more modest gatehouses.{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=474}} A third avenue to the west no longer exists, and the view to and from the Thames completes the principal approaches to the house.{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=474}} The gardens and grounds are listed Grade II* on Historic England's [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in England]].<ref name="auto"/> From the initial survey drawings produced by Robert Smythson and son in 1609,<ref name="Smythson Plan"/> it is clear that the garden design was considered as important as that of the house and that the two were intended to be in harmony.{{sfn|Strong|1979|pp=117–120}} The original design shows the house set within a range of [[walled garden]]s, each with different formal designs as well as an orchard and vegetable garden. Uncertainty remains as to how much of the original design was actually realised;{{sfn|NT|2009|p=52}} nevertheless, the plans illustrate the influence of the [[French formal garden]] of the time, with its emphasis on visual effects and perspectives.{{sfn|Anthony|1991|p=31}}

[[File:Hendrick Danckerts (1625-1680) (attributed to) - Ham House from the South (around 1675–1679) - 1139878 - National Trust.jpg|thumb|''Ham House from the South'' by [[Hendrick Danckerts]], c. 1675|alt=An oil painting showing a wide grassy avenue with trees on either side, leading to the brick south façade of Ham House, with an array of figures strolling through the gardens]]

The 1671 plans for the renovation undertaken by the Duke and Duchess of Lauderdale, which have been attributed to [[John Slezer]] and [[Jan Wyck]], demonstrate the continued importance of the garden design, with many features that exist today such as the [[Orangery]], the Cherry Garden, the [[Wilderness (garden history)|Wilderness]] and eight grass squares ([[parterre|plats]]) on the south side of the house.{{sfn|NT|2009|pp=52–54}} Both the private apartments for the Duke and Duchess and the State Apartments added to the south front of the house were designed to overlook the formal gardens, an innovation that was highly commended by contemporaries.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=113}} [[John Evelyn]] remarked favourably on the garden design observed during his August 1678 visit, noting "...the [[Parterre]]s, Flower Gardens, Orangeries, Growves, Avenues, Courts, Statues, Perspectives, Fountaines, [[Aviaries]]…".{{sfn|Evelyn|1870|p=402}} The Duchess also commissioned a set of iron gates for the north entrance to the property, which remain in place today.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=232}}

The 3rd and 4th Earls of Dysart who subsequently inherited the estate maintained the formal garden features into the 18th century, while also planting avenues of trees in the wider vicinity.{{sfn|NT|2009|p=55}} After inheriting the estate in 1799, the [[Wilbraham Tollemache, 6th Earl of Dysart|6th Earl]] opened the north front of the property to the river and installed the [[Coade stone]] statue of the River God at the front of the house.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=360}} He also created the [[ha-ha]] which runs along the north entrance of the property.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=360}} [[Louisa Tollemache, 7th Countess of Dysart]], inherited the estate upon her brother's death and was acquainted with the artist [[John Constable]], who completed a sketch of Ham House from the south gardens during a visit in 1835.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=366}}

[[File:Model of Ham House and Gardens.jpg|thumb|Miniature model of Ham House and Gardens exhibited at V&A Museum in 1974|alt=a black-and-white photograph showing a scale model of Ham House surrounded by its formal gardens, which is ringed by miniature trees]]
By 1972, the gardens had become greatly overgrown – large [[Laurus nobilis|bay trees]] at the front blocked the view of the busts in their [[Niche (architecture)|niches]], the south lawn had reverted to a single large expanse of grass and the Wilderness was overgrown with [[rhododendron]]s and sycamore trees.{{sfn|Thomas|1979|p=149}} Work to restore the 17th century design to the eastern and southern parts of the garden began in 1975.{{sfn|NT|2009|p=56}}{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=477}} In 1974, an exhibition at the [[Victoria and Albert Museum]] entitled "[[Destruction of the Country House exhibition|The Destruction of the Country House]]" had included a model of Ham House with its gardens shown according to the 1672 plans created by Ms. Lucy (Henderson) Askew.<ref name="Country Life 1975">{{cite journal |last=Jackson-Stops |first=Gervase |title=A Thames-side Parterre |journal=Country Life |date=9 October 1975}}</ref> This model illustrated the details of the 17th-century design in terms of both layout and plant selection and was used to garner support for the restoration project.<ref name="Country Life 1975" /> By 1977, the grass plats and the structure of the Wilderness to the south of the house were re-established.{{sfn|Sales|2018|p=55}} The 1675 painting by [[Hendrick Danckerts]] showing the Duke and Duchess in the south gardens was used to guide the restoration of the furniture and statues now in place.{{sfn|Sales|2018|p=56}}

In approaching the restoration of the "cherry garden" on the east side of the house, there was less documentary evidence available to guide the design.{{sfn|Sales|2018|p=56}} A set of diagonally-set parterres outlined by box hedges and cones were planted with [[lavender]], with the whole garden being enclosed by tunnel [[Pergola|arbours]] and double yew hedges.{{sfn|Sales|2018|p=57}} Later archaeological studies completed in the 1980s indicated no evidence of formal gardens in this area prior to the 20th century;{{sfn|Sales|2018|p=56}} despite this finding, the National Trust's Gardens Panel decided not to remove the garden, but rather allow it to remain so long as visitors to the property were clearly informed of its origins.{{sfn|Sales|2018|p=58}} The focus of garden restoration since 2000 has been the walled [[kitchen garden]] to the west of the house, to restore its use as a supply of fresh fruit, vegetables and flowers.{{sfn|Sales|2018|p=56}} The produce is used in the Orangery cafe, while the flowers are used to decorate the house. The garden itself is also used as an exhibition space, with information about tulip varieties and the range of edible flowers.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Garden at Ham House |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/ham-house-and-garden/features/the-garden-at-ham-house |publisher=National Trust |access-date=10 November 2021}}</ref>

==Later owners==
===Lionel Tollemache, 3rd Earl of Dysart (1698–1727)===
Elizabeth and Lionel Tollemache's eldest son and heir, [[Lionel Tollemache, 3rd Earl of Dysart|Lionel]], became 3rd Earl of Dysart on his mother's death in 1698, inheriting Ham House, the adjoining estates and the manors of Ham and Petersham.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=34}} Already the owner of his father's estates in Suffolk and Northamptonshire, he had also acquired {{convert|20000|acre|ha sqmi|lk=off}} in [[Cheshire]] through his marriage in 1680 to Grace, daughter of [[Sir Thomas Wilbraham, 3rd Baronet]].{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=34}} He only spent short periods at Ham,{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=34}} and apparently did little for the upkeep of the house though he kept the garden well.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=35}} He did use his wealth to pay off the interest on the outstanding mortgages but was not considered generous, even with his immediate family.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|pp=35–36}} His only son, Lionel, predeceased him in 1712 and on his death he was succeeded as Earl of Dysart by his grandson, also named Lionel.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=36}}

===Lionel, 4th Earl (1727–70)===
[[File:John Vanderbank (1694-1739) - Sir Lionel Tollemache (1708–1770), 4th Earl of Dysart - 1139649 - National Trust.jpg|thumb|alt=A man in courtly dress is shown standing, wearing ermine robes over a mustard-coloured jacket|Lionel Tollemache, 4th Earl of Dysart, by John Vanderbank, 1730]]
[[Lionel Tollemache, 4th Earl of Dysart|Lionel Tollemache]] was only 18 years old when he became the 4th Earl of Dysart and head of the family in 1727.  Shortly after returning from the [[Grand Tour]] in 1729 he married Grace Carteret, the 16-year-old daughter of [[John Carteret, 2nd Earl Granville]],{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=37}} and began repairing existing furniture as well as commissioning new pieces for his properties at Ham and at [[Helmingham Hall]] in Suffolk.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=37}}  Ham House had been largely neglected since the death of Elizabeth; in 1730 he ordered a structural survey of the building from [[John James (architect)|John James]] which revealed serious problems, especially on the north front.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=37}}  Repairs began in the 1740s.  At the front of the house the "Advance", a projecting [[Frontispiece (architecture)|frontispiece]] which extended two storeys to form a porch over the main entrance, had become detached from the wall and was in danger of pulling down the roof. It was removed completely and the stone reused for repairs to the first and second floors.  The [[Cant (architecture)|canted]] [[bay (architecture)|bays]] on the projections at each end of the house were rebuilt as deeper three-window bays, with corresponding alterations made to the bays on the south front. Major repairs were also made to the roof, where old unfashionable red tiles on the outer [[Roof pitch|pitches]] were replaced with [[slate]] and reused for repairs to the inner pitches where they would not be visible.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|pp=265–267}}

Much new furniture was commissioned, but the 4th Earl seems to have also been committed to preserving existing artefacts, making repairs to fixtures from the Lauderdale period where necessary.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=37}} He made three large changes to the interior of the house: the Queen's Bedchamber on the first floor became the principal drawing room with furniture and tapestries supplied by the London [[Upholstery|upholsterer]] and textile producer William Bradshaw; the Volury{{efn|The room which had been the Duchess's Bedchamber, and later the Duke's, was fitted with a set of birdcages outside the south-facing windows. The name "Volury" is thought to derive from ''volière'', the French word for birdcage.{{sfn|NT|2009|p=38}}}} on the ground floor became another drawing room with the addition of tapestries and its distinctive X-framed seat furniture; and in the Dining Room the marble floor was replaced with [[marquetry]], with matching [[gilded]] leather panels on the walls.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=290}} By means of his extensive investment, the house would have become sumptuously furnished by the mid-18th century.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=183}}

Of the sixteen children of the 4th Earl and Countess, only seven lived to maturity.{{sfn|Tollemache|1949|p=104}} Three of their five sons died in the pursuit of their naval careers.{{sfn|Tollemache|1949|p=105}} The Countess died in 1755 aged 42, and the Earl in 1770 aged 61.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=510}} He was survived by his sons Lionel, Lord Huntingtower, and Wilbraham, as well as three daughters: Jane, Louisa and Frances.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=38}}

===Lionel, 5th Earl (1770–99)===
[[Lionel Tollemache, 5th Earl of Dysart]] succeeded to the title in 1770 on his father's death.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=40}} Despite spending on the house, the 4th Earl had kept his son short of money during his lifetime, causing friction in the relationship; he married without his father's consent.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=40}} His wife, Charlotte, was the youngest illegitimate daughter of Sir [[Edward Walpole]], second son of [[Robert Walpole]], and niece of [[Horace Walpole]] who lived near to Ham across the Thames at [[Strawberry Hill House|Strawberry Hill]].{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=40}} The 5th Earl seems to have been a reclusive and introverted individual who shunned publicity,{{sfn|Walpole|2002|p=19}} preferring to remain on his estates and refusing to allow changes or renovations to Ham House.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=296}}  His aversion to visitors was so marked as to lead him to refuse a request to visit from [[George III]]; "whenever my house becomes a public spectacle, His Majesty shall certainly have the first view".{{sfn|Norwich|1985|pp=359–360}} In contrast to his conserving instincts at Ham, he demolished two properties in Northamptonshire and Cheshire, although retaining the productive, and lucrative, estates.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=360}} He continued the family tradition of acquiring fine furniture, most notably a marquetry [[commode]] which can be seen in the Queen's Bedchamber, and the sunburst chairs in the White Closet.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=41}}

Charlotte died, childless, in 1789 and although Lionel remarried he remained without an heir.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=42}} The families of his surviving sisters, Louisa and Jane, reverted to the family name of Tollemache in anticipation of eventual succession.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=360}} On his death in 1799 his brother, Wilbraham became the [[Wilbraham Tollemache, 6th Earl of Dysart|6th Earl of Dysart]].{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=43}}

===Wilbraham, 6th Earl (1799–1821)===
[[File:Father Thames, Coade stone sculpture.jpg|thumb|A close-up image of the Father Thames statue in Coade stone at the front of the house|alt=A photograph of the head and shoulders of the statue – a heavily bearded man crowned with foliage]]
Wilbraham was aged 60 when he inherited the title in 1799. One of his first acts was to buy the rights of the Manor of Kingston/Canbury from [[George Hardinge]], extending the Dysarts' property south into Kingston.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=43}} He had the wall which isolated the property and separated Ham House from the river demolished and replaced by a [[ha-ha]],{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=43}} leaving the gates free-standing. [[Coade stone]] pineapples were added to decorate the [[Baluster|balustrades]]{{sfn|Jackson-Stops|1979|p=100}} to the north of the property and [[John Bacon (sculptor, born 1740)|John Bacon]]'s statue of the river god which is placed in front of the north entrance, pictured here, also in Coade stone,{{sfn|Cherry|Pevsner|2002|p=474}} dates from this period.{{sfn|Jackson-Stops|1979|p=100}} Several [[Bust (sculpture)|busts]] of Roman emperors which had adorned the now-demolished walls since the 17th century{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=172}} were relocated to niches in the front of the house.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=44}} Further restoration of the old furniture took place as well as the addition of Jacobean reproductions.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=44}} The 6th Earl became a patron of [[John Constable]] at this time.{{sfn|Reynolds|1983|p=168}}{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=44}} Wilbraham's wife died in 1804 and, devastated, he moved away, close to the estate in Cheshire.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=44}} Wilbraham died without heir in 1821, aged 82.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=45}}

===Louisa, 7th Countess (1821–40)===
[[File:John Constable Ham House.jpg|thumb|John Constable's sketch of Ham House, June 1835|alt=A lightly rendered pencil sketch of the rear and east façades of the house]]
Of the 4th Earl's children, only the eldest daughter, [[Louisa Tollemache, 7th Countess of Dysart|Lady Louisa]], by then widow of [[John Manners (MP)|John Manners MP]], was still surviving when her brother Wilbraham, the 6th Earl, died.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=47}} Already heiress to Manners' {{convert|30000|acre|ha sqmi|lk=off}} at [[Buckminster]] Park, Louisa inherited the title and estates at Ham in 1821 at the age of 76.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=47}} The remaining Tollemache estates were bequeathed to the heirs of Lady Jane.<ref name="K58"/> Louisa continued the patronage of John Constable who was a frequent and welcome visitor to Ham.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|pp=48–49}} Increasingly infirm and blind in old age, Louisa lived to the age of 95, dying in 1840.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=50}}

===Lionel, 8th Earl (1840–1878)===
Louisa's eldest son, [[William Tollemache, Lord Huntingtower (1766–1833)|William]], had predeceased her in 1833. Her grandson, [[Lionel Tollemache, 8th Earl of Dysart|Lionel William John Tollemache]], inherited the title and became the 8th Earl of Dysart in 1840.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=370}} Lionel preferred to live in London and invited his brothers, [[Frederick Tollemache|Frederick]] and [[Algernon Tollemache|Algernon Gray Tollemache]], to manage the estates and Ham and Buckminster.{{sfn|NT|2009|p=74}} Lionel became increasingly reclusive and eccentric. Lionel's only son, [[William Tollemache, Lord Huntingtower (1820–1872)|William]], a controversial figure who amassed great debts guaranteed by the expectation of inheriting the family fortune{{sfn|NT|2009|p=74}} also predeceased his father, who subsequently bequeathed the estates to his grandson [[William Tollemache, 9th Earl of Dysart|William John Manners Tollemache]], with the 8th Earl's brothers Frederick and Algernon along with [[Sudeley Hanbury-Tracy, 3rd Baron Sudeley|Charles Hanbury-Tracy]] acting as trustees until 1899.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=371}} Following the 8th Earl's death, his son's creditors brought an action in the [[High Court of Justice|High Court]] against the Tollemache family who ultimately had to pay a sum of £70,000 to avoid forfeiting much of the Ham estate.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=370}}

===William, 9th Earl (1878–1935)===
The 9th Earl inherited in 1878. In his autobiography, [[Augustus Hare]] recounts a visit to Ham House the following year, contrasting the dilapidation and disrepair of the house and estate with the treasures the house still contained.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=189}} Shortly afterwards, the 9th Earl, with agreement from the trustees, undertook extensive renovation of the house and its contents{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=191}} and by 1885 it was again in a suitable state to host social activities, notably a garden party to celebrate the [[Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria]] in 1887. In 1890 [[Ada Sudeley]], a niece of the 8th Earl, published her 570-page book ''Ham House, Belonging to the Earl of Dysart''.{{sfn|Sudeley|1890|loc=Preface}}

On 23 September 1899, full control of the Tollemache estates at Ham and Buckminster was transferred from trustees to the 9th Earl, then aged about 40, in accordance with his grandfather's will.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=375}} By the early 1900s the Dysarts had installed electricity and central heating at the house along with other modern gadgets including, in the Duchess's basement bathroom, a bath with jets and even a wave machine.{{sfn|Thornton|Tomlin|1980|p=191}} The 9th Earl travelled widely, rode despite blindness, invested successfully in the [[stock market]], and while eccentric and difficult, nonetheless was hospitable and supportive of the local community.{{sfn|Tollemache|1949|p=130}} His cantankerous nature proved too much for his wife who left him in the early 1900s but he lived on with other family members at Ham for many years.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=375}} In the 1920s and 1930s he employed a staff of up to 20 including a chauffeur for his four cars including a [[Lanchester Motor Company|Lanchester]] and [[Rolls-Royce Limited|Rolls-Royce]]. When he died in 1935 he left investments worth £4,800,000 but had no direct heir.{{sfn|NT|2009|p=75}} He was the last Earl of Dysart to live at the house.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=384}}

===Sir Lyonel Tollemache, Bt. (1935–52)===
On the 9th Earl's death in 1935, his inheritance passed to the families of his sisters. His niece, [[Wenefryde Scott, 10th Countess of Dysart|Wynefrede]], daughter of his sister Agnes, inherited the earldom.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=63}} Wynefrede's cousin, [[Sir Lyonel Tollemache, 4th Baronet|Lyonel]], at the age of 81, inherited the [[baronet]]cy and the estates at Ham and Buckminster.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=63}} He and his middle-aged son, Cecil Lyonel Newcomen Tollemache, lived at the house, but the lack of available staff during the Second World War added to the difficulty of maintaining it. The nearby [[Hawker Siddeley]] aircraft factory was a target for bombing raids, and the house and grounds suffered some minor damage. Much of the house's contents were removed to the countryside for safety.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=63}} Most of the family papers were deposited in [[Chancery Lane]] but, while they survived [[the Blitz]], they suffered significant water damage from fire hoses.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=63}} Thought for some time to have been lost, an additional set of papers was subsequently recovered from the Ham House stables in 1953, though many were in poor condition from inadequate storage conditions.<ref name="K58"/>

===National Trust (1948–present)===
In 1943, Sir Lyonel invited the [[National Trust]]'s first Historic Buildings Secretary, [[James Lees-Milne]], to visit the house.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=384}} Lees-Milne saw the neglected state of the house and grounds but, even though devoid of its contents, the historical importance of the underlying estate was immediately apparent. He recorded his impressions in his diary for 1947, extracts from which were later reproduced in the volume ''Some Country Houses and their Owners'': "The grounds are indescribably overgrown and unkempt. All the rooms are dirty and dusty. The garden and front doors look as they had not been used for decades."{{sfn|Lees-Milne|2009|pp=33–35}} Despite the neglect, a report commissioned by Lees-Milne in 1946 concluded that it was "by far the finest, most valuable and most representative building of the period to which it belongs in the United Kingdom".{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=384}} Following lengthy negotiations, Sir Lyonel and his son donated the house and its grounds to the Trust in 1948.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|pp=385–386}} The stables and other outlying buildings were sold privately and much of the remaining estate was auctioned in 1949.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=65}}

The National Trust at first transferred ownership of Ham House to the state on a long lease to the [[Ministry of Works (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Works]].{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=66}} The contents of the house were purchased by the government who entrusted them to the [[Victoria and Albert Museum]] (V&A){{sfn|Tomlin|1985|p=75}} after considerable urging by the director of the museum, Sir [[Leigh Ashton (museum director)|Leigh Ashton]].{{efn|[[James Lees-Milne]] recorded the tortuous negotiations with [[HM Treasury]] in his diary: "After a great deal of manoeuvre I managed to insert a proviso that the N.T. should be consulted [over the] contents. The Government proposal is that they should keep the contents, and hold them through the V & A."{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1983|p=67}}}}{{sfn|Cornforth|1998|p=36}} His efforts were essential because the [[National Land Fund]], which had been established in 1946 through the sale of surplus war materials, allowed for the purchase of property but not art or other interior furnishings.{{sfn|Cornforth|1998|p=43}} The legislation was amended in 1953, following the agreement that properties such as Ham House ought to retain their historic collections.{{sfn|Cornforth|1998|p=44}}

By 1950, the house was open to the public and a series of research and restoration works since undertaken, restoring and reproducing much of the house's former grandeur.{{sfn|Pritchard|2007|p=66}} The arrival of [[Peter Thornton]] as the Keeper of the Furniture Department at the V&A led to a new approach in the management of the collection; efforts focused on arranging pieces within the house according to the documented history of the property, rather than treating individual items as simply part of the museum inventory.{{sfn|Cornforth|1998|pp=82–83}} Research on historic interiors emerged as a discipline from the late 1960s, with an important source made available through the publication of the Ham House bills and inventories in 1980.{{sfn|Cornforth|1998|p=142}}

The government relinquished its lease in 1990, and the compensation was used to form a fund to support maintenance.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bradley |first=Victoria |chapter=Ham House to the Present Day |editor-last=Pritchard |editor-first=Evelyn |title=Ham House and its Owners through Five Centuries 1610–2006 |publisher=[[Richmond Local History Society]] |location=London |year=2007 |pages=66–69 |isbn=978-1-955071-72-7}}</ref> The collections were fully transferred from the V&A to the National Trust in 2002.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=393}} Since that time, the National Trust has invested in recreating the period interiors of the house by rehanging the collection and placing furniture according to inventory records as well as commissioning replica textiles based on archival descriptions.{{sfn|NT|2009|p=76}} To celebrate the 400th anniversary of the property, a [[Academic conference|symposium]] was held to stimulate interest in new research; this led to the publication of a major historical survey overseen by Christopher Rowell in 2013.{{sfn|Rowell|2013|p=X}} The Trust continues to acquire items at auction with a historical connection to the house, such as paintings which were formerly in the collection.<ref>{{cite web |last=Bradley |first=Victoria |title=Perspectives at Ham House |url=https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/documents/abc-bulletin-summer-2016.pdf |website=National Trust ABC Bulletin |access-date=10 October 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Old Masters Evening Sale |url=https://www.christies.com/en/lot/lot-6238419 |website=Christie's |access-date=10 October 2021}}</ref> Restoration is an additional area of major investment, such as that completed for the Queen's Antechamber wallhangings in 2010.<ref>{{cite web |last=Berkouwer |first=May |title=A Forgotten Restoration. The 19th Century Restoration of the 17th Century Queen's Antechamber Wallhangings at Ham House |url=http://www.mbtexcon.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2014/03/postprint6_10-tweede-versie.pdf |website=May Berkouwer Textile Conservation |access-date=10 October 2021}}</ref> In its 2018/2019 Annual Report, the Trust reported that Ham received 127,195 visitors.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/documents/201819-annual-report.pdf|title=Annual Report 2018/19|publisher=National Trust|page=78|access-date=2 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221106000519/https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/documents/201819-annual-report.pdf|archive-date=6 November 2022}}</ref>

==Access==
The house can be reached by public transport and is located in [[Transport for London]] travel [[List of stations in London fare zone 4|zone 4]]; from [[Richmond station (London)]] the [[London Buses route 65|65 bus service]] serves Petersham Road and the 371 bus service serves Sandy Lane. These routes terminate near [[Kingston railway station (London)|Kingston station]]. There is a free council car park north-west of the house, next to the Thames. [[Hammerton's Ferry]], to the north-east, links to a playground between [[Orleans House Gallery]] and [[Marble Hill House]] below [[Twickenham]]'s central embankment. The house is accessible to pedestrians and cyclists via the [[Thames Path]] national trail.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/plan-your-visit-to-ham-house-garden|title=Plan Your Visit to Ham House Garden|publisher=National Trust|access-date=1 August 2021}}</ref>

'''Morden Hall Park''' is a [[National Trust]] park on the banks of the [[River Wandle|Wandle]] in [[Morden]], south [[London]]. Its several buildings and associated parking included, it is {{convert|125|acre}} of predominantly parkland. Hinting at the former [[leat|mill leats]] the river here splits into channels, generally, through it spanned by numerous footbridges. The estate contains '''Morden Hall''' itself, Morden Cottage, two well-preserved snuff watermills, a restored stableyard, a dog-friendly café, exhibition space and second-hand bookshop. A western part, separately accessed, hosts the National Trust's only Garden Centre.

==History==
[[File:White Bridge, Morden Hall Park.jpg|thumb|left|White Bridge, Morden Hall Park]]
[[File:Morden Hall Park 3.jpg|thumb|left|Morden Hall]]
The estate land was originally owned by [[Westminster Abbey]]. There is evidence of an earlier manor-house originally built by the Garth family where Morden Lodge now stands. The Hall dates back to the 1770s and contains a variety of natural landscapes, including the parkland of the "Deer Park", meadow and wetland. A number of historic buildings are located in the park, including the Hall itself and preserved [[watermill]]s where [[tobacco]] was once ground into [[Snuff (tobacco)|snuff]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/morden-hall-park/features/a-history-of-the-snuff-mills-at-morden-hall-park|title=A history of the snuff mills at Morden Hall Park|publisher=National Trust|access-date=9 May 2020}}</ref>

The land was occupied by the [[Morden#The Garth family|Garth family]] for generations before the estate was split in two and Morden Hall was built.
The Hall was occupied, as a school, for young gentlemen about 1840, until it was sold by Sir [[Richard Garth]] to a tobacco merchant Gilliat Hatfeild<!-- this is not a spelling mistake, the e goes before the i--> (1827–1906) in the 1870s.<ref name=nhle>{{NHLE|desc=Morden Hall Park|num=1001336|access-date=9 May 2020}}</ref>

The Hall was a military hospital during the First World War and later a Women and Children's hospital.<ref name=nhle/> Gilliat Edward Hatfeild lived at the nearby Morden Cottage.<ref name=nhle/>

Gilliat Hatfeild's son, Gilliat Edward Hatfeild (1864–9 February 1941), left the core of the estate (including the house) to the [[National Trust]], when he died.<ref name=nhle/>

Several [[Sunday Mirror#Sunday Pictorial (1915–1963)|Sunday Pictorial]] garden parties were hosted on the land in this time in aid of the [[National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children|NSPCC]] with famous British actors such as [[Richard Attenborough]], [[Alec Guinness]] and [[Patricia Roc]] in attendance.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.britishpathe.com/video/film-star-garden-party-aka-outdoor-film-festival|title=Film Star Garden Party Aka Outdoor Film Festival |year=1947|publisher=British Pathe|access-date=9 May 2020}}</ref>

==Access==
The main entrance to the park is a short walk from Morden town centre, and car parking is available in the Garden Centre car park. The Snuff Mills and Pottingshed Café are near to the main entrance.<ref name=ntacc>{{cite web | title = Morden Hall Park - Getting there | publisher = National Trust | access-date = 2 September 2008 | url = http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-mordenhallpark-2/w-mordenhallpark-gettingthere-2.htm | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080807014237/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-mordenhallpark-2/w-mordenhallpark-gettingthere-2.htm | archive-date = 7 August 2008 | df = dmy-all }}</ref>

The [[Tramlink]] [[light rail]] line from [[Wimbledon, London|Wimbledon]] to [[Croydon]], [[Elmers End]] and [[New Addington]] runs through the northern part of the park, and [[Phipps Bridge tram stop|Phipps Bridge]] and [[Morden Road tram stop|Morden Road]] tram stops give access to the park. They are respectively {{convert|0.3|mi|abbr=on}} and {{convert|0.6|mi|abbr=on}} walk through the park to the Snuff Mill and Riverside Café. [[Morden tube station]] ([[Northern line]]) and [[Morden South railway station]] ([[Thameslink (route)|Thameslink]]) are respectively {{convert|0.4|mi|abbr=on}} and {{convert|0.9|mi|abbr=on}} walk through the town centre from the main entrance.<ref name=ntacc/>
{{Clear}}

== The Living Green Project ==
Funded by the [[National Lottery Heritage Fund|Heritage Lottery Fund]] and the [[Interreg|EU's Interreg]] series of programmes, the Living Green Project was conceived as an exemplar to show how historic assets could be maintained to a highly sustainable standard.  Architects Cowper Griffiths were appointed by [[The National Trust]] along with engineers Crofton Consulting in 2009 to undertake the design with construction work commencing in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Morden Hall {{!}} Crofton|url=https://crofton.consulting/case-study/aliquam-tincidunt-mauris-eu-risus/|access-date=2020-09-30|website=crofton.consulting|language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Morden Hall Park|url=https://www.cowpergriffith.co.uk/morden-hall-park|access-date=2020-09-30|website=Cowper Griffith Architects|language=en-US}}</ref>  Receiving a [[BREEAM]] Excellent rating the project won the [[Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors|RICS]] award for Design and Innovation in 2012<ref>{{Cite web|title=Morden Hall Park Scoops RICS London Award For Sustainability|url=https://www.construction.co.uk/construction-news/144522/morden-hall-park-scoops-rics-london-award-for-sustainability|access-date=2020-09-29|website=www.construction.co.uk|language=en}}</ref> and features as a case study in the BREEAM briefing paper Sustainable Refurbishment of Heritage Buildings - How BREEAM helps to deliver.<ref>{{Cite web|last=BREEAM|date=29 September 2020|title=Sustainable Refurbishment of Heritage Buildings - How BREEAM helps deliver|url=https://tools.breeam.com/filelibrary/Brochures/Heritage-Sustainable-Refurbishment-v2.pdf|access-date=29 September 2020|website=BREEAM}}</ref>

1703335.extract: Fenton House is a 17th-century merchant's house in Hampstead in North London which belongs to the National Trust, bequeathed to them in 1952 by Lady Binning, its last owner and resident. It is a detached house with a walled garden, which is large by London standards, and features a sunken garden, an orchard and a kitchen garden. It is located on the western side of Hampstead Grove and to the south of Admiral's Walk with its entrance on Holly Hill.

It is a detached house with a walled garden, which is large by London standards, and features a sunken garden, an [[orchard]] and a [[kitchen garden]].{{refn|group=n|The plot is 1 acre (0.40 ha); its tree-lined is driveway one tenth and the house occupies 0.05 acres}} It is located on the western side of [[Hampstead Grove]] and to the south of Admiral's Walk with its entrance on [[Holly Hill, Hampstead|Holly Hill]]. ==Features== The interior houses the [[Benton Fletcher]] collection of early [[Keyboard instrument|keyboard]] instruments, some of which are often played for visitors during operational hours, and collections of paintings (including the collection of [[Peter Barkworth]] paintings), Meissen, English and Chinese [[porcelain]], 17th-century [[needlework]] pictures and [[Georgian era|Georgian]] [[furniture]]. The sides of the building feature [[balustrade]]d flat areas (parapets) above the standard decorative ledge ([[cornice]]) which date from the 18th century. The building has original staircases with twisted balusters. 1704216.title: The Carlyles' House
1704216.extract: The Carlyles' House, in Cheyne Row, Chelsea, central London, was the home of the Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher Thomas Carlyle and his wife Jane from 1834 until his death. The home of these writers was purchased by public subscription and placed in the care of the Carlyle's House Memorial Trust in 1895. They opened the house to the public and maintained it until 1936, when control of the property was assumed by the National Trust, inspired by co-founder Octavia Hill's earlier pledge of support for the house. It became a Grade II listed building in 1954 and is open to the public as a historic house museum.
